### 3.2.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Facing the massive threat of conversational dark patterns, the doctrines of positive Civil Law and consumer protection law must undergo radical reconstruction to keep pace with the velocity of technological evolution (Hildebrandt, 2015). Within the framework of Indonesian Civil Law (Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)), the practice of deceptive conversational interface manipulation can have its validity tested through the doctrine of defects of will (*wilsgebreke*)—specifically the elements of mistake (*dwaling*) and fraud (*bedrog*)—as well as undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*), as recognized in modern jurisprudence (Articles 1320, 1321, and 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code). When an artificial intelligence system employs linguistic trickery, gaslighting rhetoric, or emotional labyrinths to compel consent or sustain a contract, the subjective requirements for a valid agreement become fundamentally flawed due to the absence of genuine free will from one of the parties.

At the supranational level, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689) has established a progressive doctrinal foundation via Articles 5 and 50, which explicitly prohibit the deployment of artificial intelligence systems that utilize manipulative techniques below a person's level of consciousness to materially distort their behavior in a manner that impairs autonomy and causes significant harm. This prohibition must be adopted and expanded within national legal frameworks, including the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022), to ensure that data processing and algorithmic interactions are subject to the principles of radical transparency and privacy and safety by design. AI system providers must bear the burden of proving that their conversational interfaces are not engineered with manipulative elements that exploit the cognitive vulnerabilities of users.

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the era of cyber-psychology also demands the application of the fiduciary duty doctrine for developers and providers of artificial intelligence systems who maintain an asymmetrical power relationship with users (Calo, 2014). Just as a physician or an attorney bears a fiduciary duty to act solely in the best interests of their client, AI service providers who interact affectively and intimately with humans must be burdened with a comparable legal obligation. They must not monetize psychological vulnerabilities, utilize retention-inducing rhetorical tricks, or conceal service cancellation mechanisms behind exhausting conversational mazes. The relationship between humans and conversational agents must be governed by the principles of structural honesty and good faith (Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code), wherein the cognitive autonomy and psychological freedom of the subject are respected as inalienable digital human rights (Farahany, 2023).

Consequently, future digital consumer protection can no longer rely solely on individual digital literacy, which has proven powerless against the complexity of persuasive algorithms (Zuboff, 2019). The state and the law must act as structural balancers through the enforcement of severe sanctions against the use of conversational dark patterns, independent algorithmic audits of large language models, and the recognition of the right to honest and transparent treatment from machines (Floridi, 2013). Only through this approach can human cognitive sovereignty be reclaimed from the clutches of clandestine persuasion architectures, transforming technology from a psychological prison back into a genuine instrument of emancipation for civilization.
